def-smo-bspline.title: B-splines
def-smo-bspline.html:
Given a nondecreasing sequence κ1≤⋯≤κm+d+1, define Bj0(x)={1,κj≤x<κj+1,0,otherwise,j=1,…,m+d, and recursively, for r=1,…,d and j=1,…,m+d+1−r, Bjr(x)=ωjr(x)Bjr−1(x)+{1−ωj+1r(x)}Bj+1r−1(x),{#eq-smo-deboor}

where ωjr(x)=(x−κj)/(κj+r−κj).

A term whose denominator vanishes is read as zero. The functions B1d,…,Bmd are the B-splines of degree d on the sequence, and the matrix B with Bij=Bjd(xi) is the B-spline basis matrix of a design.

def-smo-kernel.title: Kernel weights and the local polynomial estimator
def-smo-kernel.title_html: Kernel weights and the local polynomial estimator
def-smo-kernel.html:
A kernel is a bounded function K with ∫K(u)du=1 and K(u)=K(−u), here always nonnegative and supported on [−1,1]. Its moments are μj=∫ujK(u)du and νj=∫ujK(u)2du, with R(K)=ν0. For a bandwidth h>0 write Kh(u)=h−1K(u/h).

Fix a degree q≥0. The local polynomial estimator of degree q at the point x is f^(x)=b^0, where (b^0,…,b^q) minimizes ∑i=1nKh(xi−x){yi−∑j=0qbj(xi−x)j}2.{#eq-smo-localpoly}

For q=0 this is the local constant or Nadaraya–Watson estimator f^(x)=∑iKh(xi−x)yi∑iKh(xi−x),{#eq-smo-nw}

and for q=1 the local linear estimator.

def-smo-natural.title: Natural cubic spline
def-smo-natural.html: A natural cubic spline with knots x1<⋯<xn is a function g:[a,b]→R that is a cubic polynomial on each [xi,xi+1], has two continuous derivatives on [a,b], and is linear on [a,x1] and on [xn,b]. Equivalently: on [x1,xn], g is a cubic spline with interior knots x2,…,xn−1 satisfying the natural boundary conditions g″(x1)=g″(xn)=0, extended to [a,b] by its tangent lines at x1 and xn. (The two conditions are exactly what makes the extension C2.)

def-smo-pspline.title: Penalized spline
def-smo-pspline.html:
Let B be the B-spline basis matrix of @def-smo-bspline for K interior knots, equally spaced, with K chosen generously (say 20 to 40, and in any case no more than n). For λ≥0 and an integer k≥1, the penalized spline or P-spline estimate is the function f^=∑jγ^jBjd whose coefficients minimize 𝛄𝛄𝛄𝛄𝛄‖y−Bγ‖2+λ‖Dkγ‖2=‖y−Bγ‖2+λγ⊤Pγ,P=Dk⊤Dk.{#eq-smo-pspline}

λ is the smoothing parameter and k the order of the penalty.

eq-smo-aicc.html: AICc(λ)=log⁡(‖y−f^‖2n)+1+2(df+1)n−df−2,

eq-smo-band.html: f^(xi) ± z1−α/2σ^sii.

eq-smo-clamped.html: κ1=⋯=κd+1=a,κd+1+i=ti  (i=1,…,K),κd+K+2=⋯=κm+d+1=b.

eq-smo-cv.html: CV(λ)=1n∑i=1n{yi−f^(−i)(xi)}2=1n∑i=1n(yi−f^(xi)1−sii)2,

eq-smo-deboor.html: Bjr(x)=ωjr(x)Bjr−1(x)+{1−ωj+1r(x)}Bj+1r−1(x),

eq-smo-design-bias.html: E{f^(x)}−f(x)=μ2h2{12f″(x)+f′(x)g′(x)g(x)}+o(h2).

eq-smo-df.html: df(λ)=tr(Sλ)=∑j=1m11+λej

eq-smo-mixed.html: 𝛃‖y−Xβ−Zu‖2+λu⊤u,

exm-smo-bandwidth.title: Bias, variance and the optimal bandwidth
exm-smo-bandwidth.title_html: Bias, variance and the optimal bandwidth
exm-smo-bandwidth.html:
Take n=200 equally spaced design points on [0,1] (so g≡1), σ=0.25 and f(x)=2x+e−25(x−0.35)2−34e−50(x−0.80)2, a straight line with a bump and a narrower dip. At the top of the bump, x=0.35, f″(x)=−50.06, and with the Epanechnikov kernel @eq-smo-hopt gives h∗=0.0715. Averaging 2000 data sets at each of 29 bandwidths (Figure 43.1.2), the bias at h∗ is 0.98 times the asymptotic value 12μ2f″(x)h2 and the variance 1.02 times σ2R(K)/(nh), while the empirically best bandwidth is 0.0703. For a first-order expansion at n=200 this is closer agreement than one has any right to expect.

Figure 43.1.1 shows fits at three bandwidths. At the left endpoint the two estimators part company. With h=0.08, the local constant estimator has bias 0.0938 there and the local linear estimator −0.0058, sixteen times smaller. Halving the bandwidth divides the first by 2.10 and the second by 4.38: order h against order h2, as @thm-smo-local-poly(c) says.

exm-smo-conditioning.title: Two bases for the same space
exm-smo-conditioning.title_html: Two bases for the same space
exm-smo-conditioning.html:
Take n=300 design points drawn uniformly on [0,1], cubic splines (d=3) and K=6 equally spaced interior knots, so the spline space has dimension 10. Least squares in the truncated power basis and least squares in the B-spline basis give fitted values that agree to 1.5×10−13, and the uniform sequence of the remark above agrees with the clamped one to 1.8×10−15: three bases, one fit. The condition numbers @def-mat-condition-number of the two design matrices do not agree at all — here 5.3 and 2.1×104. The table shows how they move with the number of knots.

K κ(B), B-spline κ, truncated power
5 5.3 1.25×104
10 5.8 1.08×105
20 5.5 1.01×106
40 7.4 1.45×107

Figure 43.2.1 draws the basis and a fit in it. The B-spline condition number is essentially constant; the truncated power one grows by a decade for every doubling of the knot count, and squaring it to form a cross-product matrix costs twice as many digits again (Section 6.10). At K=40 the truncated power fit has lost most of double precision, the B-spline fit a digit.

exm-smo-correlated.title: What correlated errors do
exm-smo-correlated.html:
Repeat the simulation with errors from a stationary AR(1) process of the same marginal standard deviation and autocorrelation ρ=0.7 (@def-het-ar1). The median selected degrees of freedom rise from 7.82 to 25.40 for CV, 24.53 for GCV and 23.50 for AICc, and the average squared error rises from the values just quoted to 0.04209, 0.04145 and 0.03982 — roughly a ninefold loss. The fitted curve in Figure 43.5.1(b) uses 27 degrees of freedom and traces every excursion of the error process.

There is no repair inside this section: a smooth mean and smooth-looking noise are not separately identified without an assumption about one of them. The honest responses are to model the correlation (Part VII), to choose λ by a criterion that accounts for it — leaving out whole blocks rather than single points, or REML in the mixed-model form of Section 43.6 — or to say that the wiggles are not interpretable. Opsomer, Wang and Yang (2001) survey what is known.

exm-smo-coverage.title: Measuring the coverage
exm-smo-coverage.html:
Take n=120 equally spaced points, the mean function of @exm-smo-bandwidth and σ=0.25, with a cubic P-spline on K=20 knots, so m=24 coefficients split into k=2 fixed and r=22 random ones. On one data set the transformation of @thm-smo-mixed reproduces the penalized fit to machine precision, REML chooses λ=5.01×100, which is 8.12 effective degrees of freedom, against 7.10 for GCV; the REML estimate of σ is 0.254.

Over 400 replicates, with λ re-estimated by REML each time, the nominal 95 per cent band @eq-smo-band covers f(xi) at a fraction 0.954 of the design points on average, the pointwise coverages running from 0.900 at the narrow dip near x=0.8, where the fit is most biased, to 0.985 on the flat stretches (Figure 43.6.1). The Bayesian standard errors are on average 1.12 times the naive ones of @prp-smo-linear-smoother(e), whose bands cover only 0.927 of the design points: a twelve per cent widening buys back nearly three percentage points of average coverage, and what is left over is the bias that no single width can equalize.

exm-smo-criteria.title: The three criteria on one data set, and over 200 of them
exm-smo-criteria.title_html: The three criteria on one data set, and over 200 of them
exm-smo-criteria.html:
Take n=120 equally spaced design points, the mean function of @exm-smo-bandwidth, σ=0.25, and a cubic P-spline with K=25 knots and a second-order penalty. On one data set the shortcut @eq-smo-cv agrees with 120 actual refits to 4.6×10−15, and the three criteria choose 9.83, 10.29 and 9.40 degrees of freedom.

Over 200 replicates the three are hard to tell apart. Each has median selected df 7.82, and the average n−1‖f^−f‖2 is 0.00448 for CV, 0.00449 for GCV and 0.00429 for AICc. The differences show in the upper tail: CV and GCV choose more than 15 degrees of freedom in 2.5 per cent of the samples, AICc in 0.5 per cent. The criteria are flat to the right of the minimum (Figure 43.5.1(a)), so an occasional sample sends the minimum far out, and steep to the left, so gross oversmoothing is rare.

exm-smo-knot-insensitivity.title: Nile flow, 1871 to 1970
exm-smo-knot-insensitivity.html:
The annual flow of the Nile at Aswan was recorded for 100 years from 1871 to 1970. Rescale the year to [0,1] and fit cubic P-splines with a second-order penalty. Reaching 3, 8 and 20 effective degrees of freedom needs λ=9.1×102, 4.7×100 and 1.5×10−2: five orders of magnitude for a threefold change in df, which is why λ is searched on a logarithmic scale and reported as df.

Now hold df at 8 and change the number of knots. With K=10,20,40 and 80 — the last giving 84 coefficients for 100 observations — the four curves differ nowhere by more than 16.60, or 1.82 per cent of the response range, and the K=40 and K=80 curves by at most 1.373. Without the penalty the same knot counts give curves differing by up to 258.2, fifteen times as much.

Figure 43.3.1 draws both comparisons. The fitted curve descends steeply around 1900, and it is worth saying what a smoother does and does not know: the historical record is of an abrupt change, and a smoother with a second-order penalty cannot represent a jump. It renders one as a steep smooth descent and reports no lack of fit (@thm-cor-lack-of-fit would, if the design had replicates). Smoothness is an assumption, and like every assumption in this book it buys precision by excluding something.

exm-smo-running-mean.title: The running mean
exm-smo-running-mean.html: The crudest smoother averages the responses in a window: fix a half-width h and set f^(x)=|N(x)|−1∑i∈N(x)yi with N(x)={i:|xi−x|≤h}. Three things go wrong at once. The curve is a step function, since f^ changes only when a point enters or leaves the window; every point in the window counts the same, at the centre or at the edge; and near x=a the window is one-sided, so the average estimates f somewhere to the right of a.

exm-smo-spline-fits.title: A smoothing spline, checked three ways
exm-smo-spline-fits.title_html: A smoothing spline, checked three ways
exm-smo-spline-fits.html: Take n=120 design points drawn uniformly on [0,1] and the mean function of @exm-smo-bandwidth with σ=0.25. At λ=1×10−4 the fit uses 12.32 effective degrees of freedom. Three independent computations agree with it. The roughness 𝛄𝛄γ⊤Rγ of the natural spline interpolating the true curve, 1069.5, matches ∫abg″2 from a separately constructed natural cubic interpolant to a relative error of 1.6×10−12; the banded solve @eq-smo-reinsch agrees with the dense form @eq-smo-reinsch-fit to 1.3×10−10; and minimizing 𝛄𝛄𝛄‖y−Bγ‖2+λγ⊤Ωγ over the whole space of cubic splines with a knot at every design point — dimension 122, with Ωjk=∫Bj″Bk″ computed exactly — gives fitted values differing from the smoothing spline by 4.4×10−10. That is @thm-smo-smoothing-spline in numerical form: the minimizer over the larger space is the natural spline.

exr-smo-bandwidth-matrix.title: B2
exr-smo-bandwidth-matrix.html: Show that B⊤B has (B⊤B)jk=0 whenever |j−k|>d, and deduce that a Cholesky factorization (@thm-cmp-cholesky) of B⊤B costs O(nd2) rather than O(nm2) operations. Why does the same statement fail for the truncated power basis?

exr-smo-blup-shrinkage.title: C1
exr-smo-blup-shrinkage.html: Show that in the mixed model of @thm-smo-mixed(b), the BLUP satisfies 𝛃u^=(Z⊤Z+λI)−1Z⊤(y−Xβ^), and hence that u^ is a ridge estimate (@thm-shr-ridge) on the residuals from the fixed part. Explain, using @thm-mix-blup, why the shrinkage factor is σu2/(σu2+σ2/dj2) in the jth singular direction of Z, and what happens to it as n grows with r fixed.

exr-smo-bspline-numeric.title: B1
exr-smo-bspline-numeric.html: Using the cell above, verify numerically for d=3, K=6 that ∑jBj3(x)=1, that Bj3 vanishes outside [κj,κj+4], that at most four B-splines are nonzero at any point, and that @eq-smo-greville holds. Then check @eq-smo-bderiv against a central difference.

exr-smo-count.title: A1
exr-smo-count.html: For d=3 and K=6 interior knots, write out the clamped knot sequence @eq-smo-clamped and check that it has K+2d+2 entries and yields m=K+d+1 B-splines. Which B-splines are nonzero at x=a? At the midpoint of [κ3,κ4]?

exr-smo-coverage-sigma.title: B2
exr-smo-coverage-sigma.html: @exm-smo-coverage uses σ^ from @eq-smo-sigma-hat in @eq-smo-band. Repeat the coverage simulation with σ known, and with z1−α/2 replaced by a t quantile on n−2tr(S)+tr(SS⊤) degrees of freedom. How much of the departure from nominal coverage is due to estimating σ, and how much to the bias?

exr-smo-criteria-agree.title: B2
exr-smo-criteria-agree.html: Show that log⁡GCV=log⁡(n−1‖y−f^‖2)−2log⁡(1−df/n) and that −2log⁡(1−t)=2t+t2+O(t3). Compare with @eq-smo-aicc expanded for small df/n, and explain why GCV and AIC almost always choose the same λ when n is large and differ when df is an appreciable fraction of n.

exr-smo-df-monotone.title: A1
exr-smo-df-monotone.html: Using @eq-smo-df, sketch df(λ) against log⁡λ for m=24 and a second-order penalty. What are the two horizontal asymptotes, and why is log⁡λ the right scale for the horizontal axis?

exr-smo-df-not-integer.title: B1
exr-smo-df-not-integer.html: A model with 8 parameters uses 8 degrees of freedom; a P-spline at df(λ)=8 uses 24 parameters. Explain, using @eq-smo-smoother, in what sense the two are comparable, and show that tr(SλSλ⊤)≤tr(Sλ) with equality only when Sλ is a projection. (Both traces are used as degrees of freedom in the literature; see Section 43.5.)

exr-smo-df-three.title: A1
exr-smo-df-three.html: For the projection onto a p-dimensional space, compute tr(S), tr(SS⊤) and 2tr(S)−tr(SS⊤). For a P-spline at df=8 with m=24, which of the three is largest? Using @prp-smo-linear-smoother(c), say which one the residual degrees of freedom n−2tr(S)+tr(SS⊤) subtracts.

exr-smo-efficiency.title: B2
exr-smo-efficiency.html: By @thm-smo-local-poly(d), the smallest achievable mean squared error is proportional to {μ22R(K)4}1/5. Compute this quantity for the uniform, Epanechnikov and normal kernels (for the normal, μ2=1 and R(K)=1/(2π)), and express each as a ratio to the Epanechnikov value. Conclude that the choice of kernel changes the attainable error by a few per cent, whereas @eq-smo-hopt shows that getting h wrong by a factor of two can change it by much more.

exr-smo-eigenvectors.title: C1
exr-smo-eigenvectors.html: Compute the Demmler–Reinsch basis of @lem-smo-diagonalize for a cubic P-spline with K=20, k=2, on 100 equally spaced design points, and plot u1,u2,u5,u10 against x. Confirm that e1=e2=0 and that the corresponding uj span the constant and linear functions, and that uj crosses zero more often as ej grows. Relate the picture to @eq-smo-smoother: which shapes survive a large λ?

exr-smo-flat-criterion.title: C2
exr-smo-flat-criterion.html: For the simulation of @exm-smo-criteria, record for each replicate the set of λ within one per cent of the GCV minimum, and report the median ratio of the largest to the smallest df in that set. Then plot, for one replicate, the fits at both ends of the interval. Does the choice within the flat region matter for what one would say about f?

exr-smo-gcv-invariance.title: C1
exr-smo-gcv-invariance.html: GCV was introduced by Craven and Wahba (1979) as a version of cross-validation invariant to rotation. Show that if Γ is orthogonal and one replaces y by Γy and Sλ by ΓSλΓ⊤, then GCV is unchanged while CV is not. Why is this a virtue for ridge regression (where such rotations are natural) and less obviously one for a smoother (where they are not)?

exr-smo-higher-m.title: C1
exr-smo-higher-m.html: State and prove the analogue of @lem-smo-natural-interpolant(a) for the penalty ∫ab{f(m)}2, with g a natural spline of degree 2m−1. Which boundary conditions are needed to kill the boundary terms after m integrations by parts, and what replaces “a line vanishing at n≥2 points is zero”?

exr-smo-higher-order.title: C1
exr-smo-higher-order.html:
Suppose f is four times and g three times continuously differentiable, and let K be symmetric with μ2=0 and μ4≠0 — a fourth-order kernel, which must take negative values, and which violates assumption (B).

  1. Carry @eq-smo-moment-sum two terms further, to Sn,j=nhj∑r=03hrg(r)(x)μj+r/r!+o(nhj+3), and redo the local constant (q=0) bias calculation in the proof of @thm-smo-local-poly to get E{f^(x)}−f(x)=μ4h4{f′g‴6g+f″g″4g+f‴g′6g+f(4)24}(x)+o(h4). Deduce that the optimal bandwidth is of order n−1/9 and the mean squared error of order n−8/9.

  2. Show that for q=1 the limiting moment matrix is A=diag(μ0,μ2)=diag(1,0), which is singular, so the expansion in the proof does not apply. Writing a=Sn,0, b=h−1Sn,1, c=h−2Sn,2 and ui=(xi−x)/h, show from @eq-smo-equivalent that ℓi(x)=Kh(xi−x)(c−bui)/(ac−b2), that b/c=O(h), and hence that the local linear weights collapse to the local constant ones.

  3. Why is a fourth-order kernel rarely worth using? Consider the sign of f^ when every yi≥0, the size of the constants, and (b).

exr-smo-improper-prior.title: C2
exr-smo-improper-prior.html: The prior of @thm-smo-mixed(c) is improper on N(P). Show that the posterior @eq-smo-posterior is nevertheless proper, provided BXγ has full column rank. By @exr-smo-rank-deficient that holds for k≤2 whenever the design has at least k distinct points, however the knots fall; show that it fails when it has fewer — for k=2, a design concentrated at a single x — and say what the posterior then does in the unidentified direction. Compare with the discussion of improper priors in Section 39.5.

exr-smo-interpolation-limit.title: C2
exr-smo-interpolation-limit.html: Show that if λ>0 then f^ never interpolates the data unless the data already lie on a straight line. (Use @eq-smo-reinsch-fit and the fact that Pz=0 iff z∈C([1,x]), which @exr-smo-limits establishes.) Contrast this with a regression spline with K=n−4 knots, and say what the difference means for the leave-one-out shortcut of @thm-sel-loocv.

exr-smo-limits.title: A1
exr-smo-limits.html: Show directly from @eq-smo-reinsch that f^→y as λ→0 and that f^ tends to the least squares line as λ→∞. (For the second, use @prp-smo-reinsch(b): what does Q⊤z=0 say about z?)

exr-smo-linear-exact.title: B3
exr-smo-linear-exact.html: Suppose f is exactly linear, f(x)=α+βx. Show that the local linear estimator is unbiased at every x and for every bandwidth, and that the Nadaraya–Watson estimator is unbiased at x only if ∑iKh(xi−x)(xi−x)=0. Relate the second condition to @eq-smo-design-bias.

exr-smo-marsden.title: C2
exr-smo-marsden.html: Prove that ∑jψj(y)Bjd(x)=(y−x)d for all x∈[a,b) and all y, where ψj(y)=(y−κj+1)⋯(y−κj+d), for d=0 and d=1. (This is Marsden’s identity; the general case is de Boor, 2001, ch. IX. Differentiating it d−1 times in y and setting y=x recovers @eq-smo-greville.)

exr-smo-multiplicity.title: C1
exr-smo-multiplicity.html: Suppose an interior knot is repeated ν times, 1≤ν≤d+1. Show from @eq-smo-bderiv, by induction on ν, that the B-splines are Cd−ν there, and that ν=d+1 allows a jump. How would you use this to fit a curve that is smooth everywhere except at one known breakpoint, where it is only continuous?

exr-smo-random-design.title: C2
exr-smo-random-design.html: Replace assumption (A) by: x1,…,xn are independent with density g, continuous and positive at x. Show that E{Sn,j}=nhj{g(x)μj+O(h)} and Var(Sn,j)=O(nh2j−1), so that (nhj)−1Sn,j→g(x)μj in probability. Explain why this gives the conditional bias and variance of @thm-smo-local-poly with op in place of o, and why the argument needs more care than the fixed-design one when the bias term of order h2 is required (compare the size of the stochastic error (nh3)−1/2 with h at h≍n−1/5).

exr-smo-rank-deficient.title: C2
exr-smo-rank-deficient.html: @prp-smo-pspline-ridge assumes B has full column rank, which fails if some knot interval contains no design point. Show that the minimizer of @eq-smo-pspline is still unique provided N(B)∩N(P)={0}, and give an example with K large and a gap in the design where this fails for k=1 but holds for k=2… or show that it cannot fail for k=2 either. (Hint: @thm-reg-existence(c), and the fact that N(P)=N(Dk).)

exr-smo-reinsch-check.title: B2
exr-smo-reinsch-check.html: Using the cell above, build Q and R for n=8 equally spaced points on [0,1] and verify by hand that R is tridiagonal with rjj=2h/3 and rj,j+1=h/6, and that Q⊤1=0 and Q⊤x=0. What does the second pair of identities say about Sλ1 and Sλx?

exr-smo-reml-vs-gcv.title: B1
exr-smo-reml-vs-gcv.html: Run the simulation of @exm-smo-criteria again with λ chosen by REML, and compare the median selected degrees of freedom, the average squared error and the upper tail of the df distribution with the values for CV, GCV and AICc. Which criterion is safest, and at what cost?

exr-smo-ridge-equivalence.title: B2
exr-smo-ridge-equivalence.html: Show that the P-spline criterion @eq-smo-pspline is @thm-sel-loocv’s criterion ‖y−Xb‖2+b⊤Ωb with X=B and Ω=λP, and conclude that the leave-one-out shortcut (yi−f^(xi))/(1−sii) is exact for a P-spline. What changes if the knots are chosen by looking at the data first?

exr-smo-shortcut-check.title: B1
exr-smo-shortcut-check.html: Using the cell above, verify @eq-smo-cv against n refits at three values of λ, including one so large that df≈2 and one so small that df≈m. Then do the same for a local linear estimator, using ℓi(xi) from Section 43.1.

exr-smo-shrinkage-bias.title: C3
exr-smo-shrinkage-bias.html: Assume E(Y)=f and Cov(Y)=σ2I. Using @eq-smo-smoother, show that E‖f^−f‖2=∑j(λej1+λej)2(uj⊤f)2+σ2∑j1(1+λej)2+‖(I−UU⊤)f‖2, where U=[u1,…,um]. Identify the three terms, and say which of them no choice of λ can reduce.

exr-smo-ties.title: B1
exr-smo-ties.html: Suppose the design has ties: the distinct values are t1<⋯<tN and nk observations share tk, with mean y¯k. Show that ∑i{yi−f(xi)}2=∑knk{y¯k−f(tk)}2+C with C free of f, so that @thm-smo-smoothing-spline holds with knots at the distinct values and I replaced by diag(n1,…,nN) in @eq-smo-reinsch-fit.

exr-smo-uniform-kernel.title: B1
exr-smo-uniform-kernel.html: Compute μ2 and R(K) for the uniform kernel K(u)=12 on [−1,1] and for the Epanechnikov kernel, and verify the values μ2=1/5, R(K)=3/5 quoted after @def-smo-kernel.

exr-smo-variance-ratio.title: A1
exr-smo-variance-ratio.html: Using @eq-smo-lambda-ratio, say what σu2→0 and σu2→∞ correspond to in @prp-smo-pspline-ridge, and what a REML estimate σ^u2=0 would mean about the fitted curve. Is that estimate on the boundary of the parameter space, and does @thm-mix-boundary apply?

exr-smo-weights-sum.title: A1
exr-smo-weights-sum.html: Show directly from @eq-smo-nw that the Nadaraya–Watson weights are nonnegative and sum to one, and deduce that miniyi≤f^(x)≤maxiyi. Show by example that the local linear estimator has no such property.

lem-smo-diagonalize.title: The two matrices diagonalize together
lem-smo-diagonalize.html: Suppose B has full column rank m, and let P be nonnegative definite. There is a nonsingular T with T⊤B⊤BT=I and T⊤PT=diag(e1,…,em), where 0≤e1≤⋯≤em and exactly rank(P) of the ej are positive. The columns u1,…,um of BT are orthonormal.

lem-smo-moment-sums.title: Kernel sums are integrals
lem-smo-moment-sums.html: Let φ be of bounded variation on R with support in [−1,1] and total variation V(φ). Under (A), for every x and every h>0, | ∑i=1nφ(xi−xh)−nh∫(a−x)/h(b−x)/hφ(u)g(x+hu)du |≤V(φ).{#eq-smo-riemann}

lem-smo-natural-interpolant.title: The natural interpolant, and why it is the smoothest
lem-smo-natural-interpolant.title_html: The natural interpolant, and why it is the smoothest
lem-smo-natural-interpolant.html:
Let n≥2 and x1<⋯<xn.

  1. If g is a natural cubic spline with these knots and h∈W satisfies h(xi)=0 for every i, then ∫abg″h″=0.

  2. For every z∈Rn there is exactly one natural cubic spline g with g(xi)=zi; the space of natural cubic splines with these knots has dimension n.

  3. That g is the unique minimizer of ∫abf″2 among all f∈W with f(xi)=zi.

prp-smo-bayes-bands.title: Wahba–Nychka bands
prp-smo-bayes-bands.html:
Let Sλ=B(B⊤B+λP)−1B⊤ with diagonal entries sii.

  1. Under @thm-smo-mixed(c), 𝛄f(xi)=Bi⋅γ has posterior distribution N(f^(xi),σ2sii), giving the Bayesian band f^(xi) ± z1−α/2σ^sii.{#eq-smo-band}

  2. sii≥(SλSλ⊤)ii, so @eq-smo-band is never narrower than the interval of @prp-smo-linear-smoother(e), and is strictly wider unless Sλ is a projection.

  3. (Stated, not proved.) Treating f as fixed, the extra width in (b) accounts approximately for the squared bias, in the sense that n−1∑iσ2sii approximates n−1∑i[Var{f^(xi)}+bias{f^(xi)}2] when λ is near its risk-optimal value. Consequently the average over the design points of the coverage of @eq-smo-band is close to 1−α, while the coverage at any single xi is not: it is below nominal where f curves sharply and above it where f is nearly straight. This is across-the-function coverage (Wahba, 1983; Nychka, 1988).

prp-smo-bspline.title: Properties of the B-spline basis
prp-smo-bspline.html:
Let B1d,…,Bmd be as in @def-smo-bspline. Then:

  1. (Local support.) Bjd(x)=0 for x∉[κj,κj+d+1), and, for the sequence @eq-smo-clamped with distinct interior knots, Bjd(x)>0 for κj<x<κj+d+1. In particular at most d+1 of the Bjd are nonzero at any point.

  2. (Nonnegativity.) Bjd≥0 everywhere.

  3. (Partition of unity.) For the sequence @eq-smo-clamped, ∑j=1mBjd(x)=1 for every x∈[a,b).

  4. (Piecewise polynomial.) On each interval between consecutive distinct knots, Bjd is a polynomial of degree at most d.

  5. (Derivative.) For d≥1, ddxBjd(x)=d{Bjd−1(x)κj+d−κj−Bj+1d−1(x)κj+d+1−κj+1},{#eq-smo-bderiv}

    with the same convention on zero denominators. Consequently Bjd has d−1 continuous derivatives at every simple knot.

  6. (Basis.) For the sequence @eq-smo-clamped with distinct interior knots, B1d,…,Bmd are linearly independent on [a,b] and span the spline space of @thm-ply-spline-space, of which they are therefore a basis. (With a repeated interior knot they span a larger space, one with a weaker continuity requirement there; see @exr-smo-multiplicity.)

prp-smo-equivalent-kernel.title: Equivalent kernel weights
prp-smo-equivalent-kernel.html:
Suppose Ux⊤WxUx is nonsingular. Then f^(x)=∑iℓi(x)yi with ℓi(x)=e1⊤(Ux⊤WxUx)−1Ux⊤Wxei,{#eq-smo-equivalent}

where e1 is the first standard basis vector, and

  1. ∑iℓi(x)(xi−x)j=δj0 for j=0,…,q, where δj0 is one if j=0 and zero otherwise;

  2. consequently f^ reproduces polynomials: if f is a polynomial of degree at most q then ∑iℓi(x)f(xi)=f(x) for every x, whatever the design, the kernel and the bandwidth;

  3. the weights do not depend on y, so Var{f^(x)}=σ2∑iℓi(x)2.

prp-smo-greville.title: Greville abscissae
prp-smo-greville.html:
Let ξj=(κj+1+⋯+κj+d)/d for j=1,…,m, the Greville abscissae of the sequence. For @eq-smo-clamped, ∑j=1mξjBjd(x)=xfor all x∈[a,b].{#eq-smo-greville}

Consequently ∑j(α+βξj)Bjd(x)=α+βx: coefficients that are an affine function of the Greville abscissae produce an affine function of x.

prp-smo-linear-smoother.title: Linear smoothers
prp-smo-linear-smoother.html:
Call f^=Sy a linear smoother with smoother matrix S when S does not depend on y. The estimators of @def-smo-kernel, @def-smo-pspline and @thm-smo-smoothing-spline are linear smoothers, with S given by @eq-smo-equivalent, @eq-smo-smoother and @eq-smo-reinsch-fit. Suppose E(Y)=f and Cov(Y)=σ2I. Then:

  1. (Moments.) E(f^)=Sf, Cov(f^)=σ2SS⊤, and E‖f^−f‖2=‖(I−S)f‖2+σ2tr(SS⊤).{#eq-smo-risk}

  2. (Residuals.) E‖y−f^‖2=‖(I−S)f‖2+σ2{n−2tr(S)+tr(SS⊤)}, so σ^2=‖y−f^‖2n−2tr(S)+tr(SS⊤){#eq-smo-sigma-hat}

    is unbiased for σ2 when the bias term is negligible.

  3. (Degrees of freedom.) If S is symmetric with eigenvalues in [0,1] — as it is for a penalized or smoothing spline, by @prp-smo-pspline-ridge(b) — then tr(SS⊤)≤tr(S)≤2tr(S)−tr(SS⊤), with equality throughout iff S is an orthogonal projection, in which case all three equal its rank.

  4. (Shrinkage.) For a penalized spline, @eq-smo-smoother writes Sλ in the Demmler–Reinsch basis as a diagonal shrinkage uj⊤y↦uj⊤y/(1+λej): smooth directions (ej small) pass through, rough ones are damped. The smoothing spline has the same form with ej the eigenvalues of the roughness matrix relative to the identity.

  5. (Pointwise bands.) f^(xi)±z1−α/2σ^(SS⊤)ii is an interval for E{f^(xi)}=(Sf)i, not for f(xi). Its coverage of f(xi) is 1−α only to the extent that the bias {(S−I)f}i is small next to σ(SS⊤)ii.

prp-smo-penalty-limit.title: The limiting fit
prp-smo-penalty-limit.html:
Let Dk be the kth difference matrix.

  1. 𝛄N(Dk)={γ:γj=p(j) for a polynomial p of degree<k}, of dimension k.

  2. For k=1, the limiting fit of @prp-smo-pspline-ridge(c) is the constant y¯, whatever the knots.

  3. For k=2 and equally spaced Greville abscissae (@prp-smo-greville) — the uniform knot sequence of Section 43.2 — the limiting fit is the ordinary least squares line.

prp-smo-pspline-ridge.title: A P-spline is a ridge regression
prp-smo-pspline-ridge.title_html: A P-spline is a ridge regression
prp-smo-pspline-ridge.html:
Let B have full column rank and λ>0, and write T,ej,uj as in @lem-smo-diagonalize.

  1. 𝛄γ^=(B⊤B+λP)−1B⊤y is the unique minimizer of @eq-smo-pspline, and the fitted vector is f^=Sλy with Sλ=B(B⊤B+λP)−1B⊤=∑j=1m11+λejujuj⊤.{#eq-smo-smoother}

  2. Sλ is symmetric with eigenvalues (1+λej)−1∈(0,1] and the same eigenvectors for every λ. Its effective degrees of freedom — the count of @thm-shr-ridge(b), now for a roughness penalty — df(λ)=tr(Sλ)=∑j=1m11+λej{#eq-smo-df}

    decrease strictly and continuously from m at λ=0 to m−rank(P) as λ→∞. For a kth-order difference penalty, rank(P)=m−k, so the limit is k.

  3. As λ→∞, Sλ tends to the orthogonal projection onto C{BN(P)}, a space of dimension k.

prp-smo-reinsch.title: Band matrices for the roughness
prp-smo-reinsch.html:
Let hi=xi+1−xi for i=1,…,n−1, and let n≥3. Define Q, of size n×(n−2), and R, symmetric tridiagonal of order n−2, by qj−1,j=1hj−1,qj,j=−1hj−1−1hj,qj+1,j=1hj, rjj=hj−1+hj3,rj,j+1=rj+1,j=hj6, for j=2,…,n−1 (columns and rows indexed by the interior knots), all other entries zero. Then:

  1. R is positive definite.

  2. If g is the natural cubic spline with values z and 𝛄γ={g″(x2),…,g″(xn−1)}⊤, then 𝛄Rγ=Q⊤z and 𝛄𝛄∫abg″2=γ⊤Rγ, so that P=QR−1Q⊤.

  3. The fit of @thm-smo-smoothing-spline satisfies 𝛄𝛄(R+λQ⊤Q)γ^=Q⊤y,f^=y−λQγ^,{#eq-smo-reinsch}

    and R+λQ⊤Q has bandwidth two, so the fit costs O(n) operations.

thm-smo-lambda.title: Cross-validation, generalized cross-validation and AIC for smoothers
thm-smo-lambda.title_html: Cross-validation, generalized cross-validation and AIC for smoothers
thm-smo-lambda.html:
Let Sλ be the smoother matrix, f^=Sλy, df=tr(Sλ) and sii the diagonal entries of Sλ — the leverage of @prp-proj-leverage and Section 20.2, read now for a smoother instead of a projection.

  1. (The leave-one-out shortcut is exact.) For a penalized spline and for a smoothing spline, CV(λ)=1n∑i=1n{yi−f^(−i)(xi)}2=1n∑i=1n(yi−f^(xi)1−sii)2,{#eq-smo-cv}

    where f^(−i) is the fit computed without case i at the same λ. The same identity holds for a local polynomial estimator, with sii=ℓi(xi).

  2. (Generalized cross-validation.) Replacing each sii by the average df/n gives @def-sel-gcv, GCV(λ)=n−1‖y−f^‖2(1−df/n)2,{#eq-smo-gcv}

    which needs only the trace, and satisfies GCV=n−1‖y−f^‖2(1+2df/n)+O(df2/n2).

  3. (Information criteria.) Under normal errors with σ2 profiled out, @prp-sel-aic-bic gives AIC(λ)=nlog⁡(‖y−f^‖2/n)+2df. Its small-sample correction (Hurvich, Simonoff and Tsai, 1998) is AICc(λ)=log⁡(‖y−f^‖2n)+1+2(df+1)n−df−2,{#eq-smo-aicc}

    which penalizes large df much more heavily and has a pole at df=n−2.

  4. (What they estimate.) If Cov(Y)=σ2I, then E{CV(λ)} is, up to O(n−1) terms, the average prediction error at a fresh response, which exceeds n−1 times the risk @eq-smo-risk by σ2. A minimizer of any of the three is therefore aiming at @eq-smo-risk, not at λ itself, and nothing here estimates a “true” smoothing parameter, since no such thing is assumed to exist.

thm-smo-local-poly.title: Bias and variance of a local polynomial estimate
thm-smo-local-poly.title_html: Bias and variance of a local polynomial estimate
thm-smo-local-poly.html:
Assume (A)–(D) and let x satisfy [x−h,x+h]⊂(a,b).

  1. (Local linear, q=1.) E{f^(x)}−f(x)=12μ2f″(x)h2+o(h2),Var{f^(x)}=σ2R(K)nhg(x){1+o(1)}.

  2. (Local constant, q=0.) The variance is the same to first order, and E{f^(x)}−f(x)=μ2h2{12f″(x)+f′(x)g′(x)g(x)}+o(h2).{#eq-smo-design-bias}

  3. (At the boundary.) Let x=a+ch with c∈[0,1) fixed, and write μj,c=∫−c1ujK(u)du. Then the local constant estimator has bias f′(a)hμ1,c/μ0,c+O(h2), of exact order h unless f′(a)=0, while the local linear estimator still has bias O(h2).

  4. (Optimal bandwidth.) For the local linear estimator with f″(x)≠0, the pointwise mean squared error 14μ22f″(x)2h4+σ2R(K)/{nhg(x)} is minimized at h∗(x)={σ2R(K)g(x)μ22f″(x)2}1/5n−1/5,{#eq-smo-hopt}

    and the minimum value is 54{μ22f″(x)2}1/5{σ2R(K)/g(x)}4/5n−4/5.

thm-smo-mixed.title: A penalized spline is a linear mixed model
thm-smo-mixed.title_html: A penalized spline is a linear mixed model
thm-smo-mixed.html:
Let P be nonnegative definite of order m and rank r=m−k, write P=LL⊤ with L of size m×r and full column rank, let Xγ be m×k with columns spanning N(P), and set Zγ=L(L⊤L)−1.

  1. (The transformation.) [Xγ,Zγ] is nonsingular, so every 𝛄γ is uniquely 𝛄𝛃γ=Xγβ+Zγu; moreover 𝛄u=L⊤γ and 𝛄𝛄γ⊤Pγ=u⊤u.

  2. (The mixed model.) With X=BXγ and Z=BZγ, the P-spline criterion @eq-smo-pspline is 𝛃‖y−Xβ−Zu‖2+λu⊤u,{#eq-smo-mixed}

    which is the penalized criterion @eq-mix-penalized of the linear mixed model 𝛃𝛆Y=Xβ+Zu+ε, u∼Nr(0,σu2I), 𝛆ε∼Nn(0,σ2I) independent, with λ=σ2/σu2.{#eq-smo-lambda-ratio}

    Its solution is Henderson’s (@thm-mix-henderson): 𝛃β^ is the generalized least squares estimate and u^ the BLUP (@thm-mix-blup).

  3. (The Bayesian reading.) Suppose σ2 is known and 𝛄γ has the prior with density proportional to 𝛄𝛄exp⁡{−γ⊤Pγ/(2τ2)}, τ2=σ2/λ — equivalently 𝛃β flat and u∼Nr(0,τ2I). Then 𝛄𝛄γ∣Y=y ∼ Nm{γ^, σ2(B⊤B+λP)−1},{#eq-smo-posterior}

    with 𝛄γ^ the penalized estimate of @prp-smo-pspline-ridge(a).

  4. (REML.) The marginal distribution is 𝛃Y∼Nn(Xβ,σ2Vλ) with Vλ=I+λ−1ZZ⊤. Profiling σ2 out of the restricted likelihood (@def-mix-reml, @thm-mix-reml) leaves −2ℓR(λ)=(n−k)log⁡σ^λ2+log⁡|Vλ|+log⁡|X⊤Vλ−1X|+c,{#eq-smo-reml}

    where σ^λ2=y⊤Aλy/(n−k) with Aλ=Vλ−1−Vλ−1X(X⊤Vλ−1X)−1X⊤Vλ−1, and c does not depend on λ. Minimizing @eq-smo-reml over λ>0 estimates the smoothing parameter.

thm-smo-smoothing-spline.title: The smoothing spline
thm-smo-smoothing-spline.html:
Let λ>0 and n≥2 distinct design points. Then Sλ of @eq-smo-variational has a unique minimizer over W, and it is the natural cubic spline with knots at x1,…,xn whose vector of values is f^=(I+λP)−1y,{#eq-smo-reinsch-fit}

where P is the nonnegative definite matrix representing the roughness, ∫abg″2=z⊤Pz, of the natural cubic spline with values z.
